utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Matthew Olmsted, Thomas Laugel, and Kathryn Fox.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Today I would like us to conclude with the issue concerning the uniforms that we were talking about yesterday. You saw the video, and the video showed some women who were complaining to some soldiers. They were complaining about members of the Croatian forces who hadn't treated Serbs correctly. I'm interested in being told what type of uniforms they had. Could you tell us what uniforms you saw on those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the hearing I remembered something. First you asked about the Territorial Defence, about the uniforms it had. That was before 90 -- 1991, and you asked about the active-duty JNA and also JNA reservists. The reserve forces of the JNA had the same uniforms as the JNA, as per establishment at the time, but your question was certainly about the uniforms that they had on the battle-field, and that is where the problem arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is at stake, in fact, because I'm, in fact, interested in the uniforms that were used in the course of the combat activity in the second part of 1992 [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, gentlemen, you're overlapping. It doesn't work. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the second half of 1991 - I see that the transcript says, 1992 - that's what I'm interested in, not the period prior to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All JNA units that were mobilised came to the battle-field, and they were provided with same types of uniforms. In the course of the combat operations, those who sustained losses, for example, or if there were certain individuals who weren't fit for combat or weren't psychologically fit, they would be replaced. There were people who came from the Teosid [phoen]. They came with TO uniforms, and they were made part of the JNA. So there were olive-drab uniforms that were worn within the JNA forces at the time of combat operations, at the time of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday you spoke about the meeting that was held in Velepromet on the 20th of November, 1991. Sir, could you please tell me if I've understood you correctly, when you arrived at Velepromet you didn't know that the members of the government would be coming. It's only when you met up with Vojnovic that you discovered this.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As the surname Vojnovic concerns three individuals, I will tell you which individuals the name concerns, the surname concerns, so that we're quite sure about the individual we are referring to. Please listen to me carefully. We know that there was a Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, who was the commander of the 80th Brigade and was subsequently the commander of the town of Vukovar. Secondly, we also known that there was a Bogdan Vojnovic who was a minister in the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. There was a Milos Vojnovic who was the president of the court and before the war he was also a judge. So I'm interested in knowing which Vojnovic you spoke to. I have understood you, but I would like us to be clear for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Milos Vojnovic, the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us about that conversation you had with him. What I'm interested in is whether he told you or whether you came to the conclusion somehow about the reasons for which he was contacting you and sending you to see Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was because only I went to Mrksic's meetings as the commander of the Petrova Gora detachment, and none of the members from the government had any contact with them. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say with him, you mean with Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this perhaps also the reason for which later on Goran Hadzic asked you to exert your influence in order to establish civilian authorities in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran didn't tell me whom I was to influence. He just said that we should try to make this happen, to try to influence this. He didn't say whether we should influence Mrksic or someone else. I wasn't told where to have meetings and whom to speak to. It was just a matter of using our authority, and it was just a matter of establishing civilian administration that was to replace the military one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that for a short period of time you were at this meeting that was held in Velepromet. I would now like to show you a photograph of the Velepromet feature, panoramic photograph, but could you tell us where this meeting was held, the one that you partially attended? [In English] 2802, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a hundred per cent certain about this to the right --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a pen, could you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does it matter if I use this pen to mark it? We have offices here, and this is where the TO staff was, in those offices. Now, I'm not a hundred per cent certain. It's -- 22 years have passed since then. At the end of the hall in the offices, I don't know if there is a corridor and then that room. I don't know whether it's there or opposite. I'm not quite sure, but here to the right that is where the room was, and I assume that here at the end of the corridor leading from the offices there was a larger corridor and then a large room. I think that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to mark the larger circle with the letter K, or mark it with the letters TO, if you like.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you mark the smaller circle with H for "hall" or "room."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You saw the photograph of you and Goran Hadzic and some other people you recognised. Could you tell me roughly in relation to this photograph where was that photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in the yard. I don't know where exactly. You can probably see by looking at the photograph that it was in the -- in the Velepromet yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You could mark that with the letter V for "video."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D88, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Having spoken to Vojnovic -- and that was before the meeting in Velepromet, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After that conversation you went to see Lieutenant-Colonel Mrksic. You said that you had returned. Did you then go to Velepromet and to the room where that meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to the room, told Vojnovic what Mrksic had said, and while I was doing this I remember that there was some sort of euphoria concerning the army, amongst the army members, and then I went to Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You've said so. When you say there was a certain euphoria concerning the army, what was all this about? Do you remember? What were they saying about the army? Why did they criticise the army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was because they said that the army was protecting war criminals who had perpetrated massacres, who had been involved in killing people. So very briefly I remember that there was this sort of excitement because of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there anything said about the situation in Vukovar itself, about the destruction of the town?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And please tell me, do you remember were there any army representatives present who -- to whom such criticisms were directed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of people in the room. I don't remember any of them in the room, but before the meeting I think I saw -- I remember I saw Sljivancanin in the corner of the room. As to whether he actually attended the session, the meeting, I cannot remember, because there were a lot of people and they were all in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember that you testified in the Mrksic case. It was at the hearing held on the 15th of September, 2006. 4694, 65 ter is the exhibit number -- rather it's a 65 ter document, 4694. I'll just read out a passage that concerns this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have a page, transcript page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. [Interpretation] I think it's page 9. It's page 57. My apologies. It's page 57. I don't seem to be able to find the page. Let me try again. I am definitely unable to locate it at this time. I have the text though.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would request the Defence counsel find the page just so that I'm able to follow along in the transcript with him. Perhaps he can come back to this after he's figured out the correct transcript page. I don't need to see it on the screen. I just need the transcript page in the Mrksic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It seems a reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best to find it, indeed, and I'll not ask the witness about it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, it is your evidence now that you did not see Sljivancanin at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing him in the meeting. There were many uniformed people. It was a crowd. I did see him in the room, but I can't state for a fact that he was there later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you did see Vukasinovic in -- in his company?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During this exchange in that room, do you recall there being present a JNA officer who presented views that were contrary to those of the others?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for a short time. I don't recall that. I don't recall that any of the officers spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that there was an officer present at all?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do remember that they were all in uniform. What mattered to me was to meet with Vojnic and convey the message to him, and then I left. I did not pay attention to whether there were any officers around. They were all in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they were all in uniform --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even those who were the TO, those who were locals, those who were supposed to be there, those who weren't supposed to be there, they were all in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they had uniforms, you mean military uniforms, the olive-drab uniforms.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were even some territorials who already had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But they were also olive green, were they not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that after the meeting you went to Petrova Gora. You said that Goran Hadzic was in a car driving behind you. You were also asked by the Prosecutor about the time when the sun set at the time.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you a document precisely about this. It's 1D480. It's a document that was obtained from the astronomy institute. You'll have a look at it, and it does state the time when the sun sets in quite precise terms. What you can see here is a report received from the astronomic observatory. It sets out the times of sunrise and twilight, and that's for the dates of 17, 18 -- that's to say 19, 20, and 21st November 1991, specifically for the place of Grabovo. Do you know where Grabovo is located approximately?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, it's somewhere in the direction of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see the column in the middle. The date is the 20th of November. You see the beginning of daylight, sunrise, sunset. It's 16.11, that is to say 4.11 in the afternoon, and then the end of twilight, 16.43. Is that typical, would you say, of that part of year?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the second half of November the day grows much shorter. That much is known. I didn't know, of course, these parameters, but I did say it was around 5.30, and here it says around 5.00. So that's roughly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D89, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I suppose when the time comes for submissions we would hear what you would invite the Chamber to make of this, but looking at it now, I'm wondering whether to what extent things like cloud cover are taken in account of and, therefore, what utility this report made years after the fact would be, but no doubt we would hear from you at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that they took into account clouds and all these factors, but it is indication when is sunset and when is usual time when the dark is at the time at this specific location, and in our submission it could be very, very important for -- for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point the Prosecution's not taking any position regarding that. We can see the information. It's not disputing it at this point, but we would disagree with Mr. Zivanovic's conclusion that it factors in clouds and other factors as this is from the astronomy institute and therefore it appears to be simply looking at when technically the sun had set and when twilight would technically end without taking in weather conditions, because there is no mention of that in this document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: All that is on the record now. Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've managed to find your evidence. It's 4694, and the page is 31. Or 11973. That's the exact page of the transcript. It's line 11. I'll read this out for you since it's in English and you will receive interpretation: [In English] "Q. Yesterday you said that you saw Mr. Sljivancanin at the government session, and you said you were there very briefly. Tell me: Where did you see him, and what was he doing at the government session? "A. He was with Vukasinovic. He was standing on the side when I saw him in the hall, when I saw him there." [Interpretation] My impression of this answer is that you stated that you did see Sljivancanin during the government meeting there.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Mr. Vojnovic before the government meeting began, although we were in the same room, but the government meeting had not started yet, and that was when I saw them. So I did see him in that same room. After that I went to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not speak to Sljivancanin or Vukasinovic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you did go to Vukovar later on, do you know for how long did the military administration remain in town?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically. I think for a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who the commander of the Vukovar was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel Vojnovic. I think his first name was Milorad, if my memory serves me well, though I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him on this day, the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During these combat operations and as long as the Petrova Gora detachment existed, do you remember if members of the Petrova Gora detachment received any sort of reimbursement for their engagement, let's say, a salary?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All members of the TO, including the Petrova Gora detachment; for instance, Luzac was under the entire operations group. All those who were there either within the Operations Group North or South received their salaries from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what period this applied to, although you did leave early year on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I left earlier on, but I'm sure that this situation prevailed for at least another month.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you discussed various events in Vukovar prior to the outbreak of conflicts. Reviewing your earlier evidence, I saw that you were once involved in an incident with individuals who sported the Ustasha insignia. Can you tell us something more specific about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened after I had exhausted my annual leave and when I reported for my first day of work. Now, on that day we were released early from work at around noon. Since there were no more Serbs at work, tensions were high. There were no buses running outside of Vukovar, and therefore there was no need for us to work for longer than one shift. On the road in the direction of Djergaj there's a bridge. That's where the ZNG and police had a check-point. They pulled us over there. The policeman took the IDs of all three of us. He then motioned to a ZNG member to join him. The ZNG member started harassing the driver. What I saw then was on his left jacket pocket of his uniform and there was a large bronze sign as large as the pocket itself. It had a large U, and beneath it read "The Ustasha Renaissance" or "awakening."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that Petrova Gora, the neighbourhood itself, was predominantly inhabited by the Serbs, although there were other ethnicities present. When the Petrova Gora detachment was set up, did it consist of Serbs only or were there members of other ethnicities? And we're talking about the time when the hostilities had already broken out, September and later.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Ruthenians, Croats, Italians, and they all joined the TO voluntarily. I know there was someone whose nickname was Medo. I can't his first and last name now. I know that he worked in Trpinje, in a collective for agricultural products. He was with us throughout the wartime period. After liberation, he could have stayed on, but he decided to leave. He had family in Croatia, so he went perhaps to Zagreb. I can't remember exactly where, and later we heard from his neighbours or, rather, his mother, that they had sent him to the battle-field in Bosnia and that he had been killed by Croats from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the commanders of TO companies, you also mentioned the command of the 4th Company, I believe, Sinisa Fot was his name. Tell me, was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa Fot was a Croat who attended all the meetings, and he was a fervent supporter of Yugoslavia. After those meetings he was arrested by the Croats in town and tortured by them. They broke his collarbone, and after that he joined us and he was a real fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to him in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed on the 2nd October when the Guards Brigade launched an attack somewhere near Dalmatinska Street to the right of the barracks. Well, the streets in that neighbourhood are very narrow. There was no shelter. He had a flak jacket on him, but a sniper bullet hit him just below the armpit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I also saw the name Darko Fot. Could you tell us whether he a Serb or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was his elder brother. He was also seriously wounded that day. He was wounded in the stomach, but he survived and works in Novi Sad for the customs office. They managed to get him out of the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the footage of Velepromet, you also recognised Rade Kosic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Kosic. Vlado Kosic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is Vlado Kosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of work he did?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that later he became the director of the water supply company. I know he worked in Save Kovacevica Street and I was with my brother in Vasilje Gica. So he was one street down. I was staying with my brother until I got married.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecution mentioned someone called Bibic, and then two names appeared, Rajko or Srbobran.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos. Everyone called him Rajko. I can't say that his actual name wasn't Srbobran, but everyone called him Rajko. I never heard anyone calling him Srbobran.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because perhaps there are several Bibics. Perhaps they are two different individuals.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they both worked in the agricultural collective, Rajko was the director, and Milos was a reserve officer and had some sort of work in the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the same document that is on the screen now, but the page, I believe, is 14. Fourteen. Amongst other things, if I -- if I understood you correctly, you said that at that meeting in Velepromet the army was asked to establish a civilian authority structure. I'll try and find the place now. I think it's on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Or page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- I was going to say I think it was on the previous page. If the Defence counsel is referring to the witness's conversation with Mr. Hadzic, it's on transcript page 11955.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. I think that it was said in another context. It is this page, line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read what it says in the transcript: [In English] "Q. Mr. Jaksic, explain something for all of us here. Pressure exerted on the army, what does this mean exactly? Tension against the army, what does this mean exactly? "A. This was to make the military administration transform into a civilian government, and, in part, it had to do with the prisoners. I can't remember all the details." [Interpretation] Do you remember that that was your answer, the pressure for civilian authorities to be established was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This had to do with war criminals being put on trial. The civilian authority should do so. The army wasn't to transfer them to Serbia. Civilian organs were to function. The judiciary was to put them on trial. So that is the context. That is what the issue was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But don't you remember who was against this idea at the meeting? Did someone or did anyone say, No, we can't do this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. There's a lot of noise from all sides. I didn't hear one individual standing up and speaking. Everyone was speaking. There was a lot of commotion all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, you didn't stay until the end of the meeting. You told Vojnovic what Mrksic had told you and then you left.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And one other thing. When you spoke about your shift after Milovo Brdo fell on the 16th or 17th of November, you said that Sljivancanin informed you of this decision. Did you wonder how it is that Sljivancanin as the chief of security -- he wasn't the commander to whom you were subordinated. Did you wonder why he was informing you of such a decision instead of Mrksic who was, in fact, your superior?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the command and the security organ represented authority in the area, in the area of responsibility of that unit, and Sljivancanin was responsible for the Guards Brigade, well, these two individuals knew each other quite well, and I thought that Mrksic would then say that he would accept the decision. I was there for a month and a half with Mrksic, but he was there throughout his tour of duty while he was serving in the army, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't ask for any explanation as to why it was decided. It was only later that you came to those conclusions. In other words, you never asked Mrksic why this occurred.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the reasons last time. That wasn't the only reason. It was also because my life was threatened. I had received information from the Military Intelligence Service according to which they were preparing to eliminate me, and that's why I accepted this. I was an obstacle. I transferred my power to them and I no longer had a role of any kind to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you receive this information according to which they were preparing to eliminate you? How many days prior to the time when you were replaced, for example?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. There were these six trailers for humanitarian aid for Vukovar which arrived, and when I asked where they had gone, why they hadn't been unloaded in Vukovar, when I asked who signed the relevant document, they then started harassing me, and Sljivancanin then started an operations procedure. Then I asked about the troops in Sid and why they were there. I had certain information. I also raised this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you raised this issue concerning the trailer --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six trailers. Six trailer trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Six trailer trucks. With whom did you raise this issue? Did you tell anyone about this? Did you ask anyone to launch an investigation to determine what had happened to these trailer trucks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first raised the issue in Velepromet. I wanted to find out who had signed this fake document and who had authorised them to just turn around in Velepromet and return to Serbia. I then informed the high-level command of the fact and after liberation I heard that they were accompanied by Dusan Spasojevic, also known as Siptar, who was eliminated or killed in the Sablja operation. He brought them in and he was their cover. He had an important role in the state, and Sljivancanin probably had an agreement with him, and they then launched this harassment campaign depends me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you raised this issue at a high-level command, did you have the OG south in mind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You followed the same procedure with regard to the cigarettes for the troops.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cigarettes or the right amount of cigarettes didn't arrive. I then asked what had happened with the cigarettes from Sid. Why had someone taken cigarettes that were intended for the troops? We knew how many cigarettes were to arrive and not even 50 per cent of the cigarettes had arrived. I also raised this issue. And in Sid, in the staff I suppose someone launched a campaign against me, and there was this slander, these lies. They attributed their actions to me and they accused me of black marketeering with cars. They said that I had a lot of euros in bank accounts and I was very much affected by this. When you know that you are honest, this is psychologically very damaging.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, since you raised all these issues you were warned about the fact that there were preparations underway for you to be killed.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This happened --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Velepromet when I was going to the kitchen from the staff, and in front of the kitchen there is a wall, and a sniper bullet just missed me and hit the wall. I thought it was a stray bullet. When I returned a bullet whizzed by behind my crown. I was then aware of what was going on. I relinquished my duties, the power I had. I knew I was an obstacle to them, and I knew I couldn't survive there. There was a lot of crime. I couldn't be part of their circle. This was against my conscience, so I quite simply withdrew to lead a peaceful life. I relinquished all the power that I had and I moved over to a company, and I no longer participated as a member of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing. You said that you were being accused of various misdeeds. There's no need to reiterate them. Was a court proceeding ever instituted against you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wish it had been, because then the truth would have come out sooner. I was contemplating a lawsuit against Mr. Sljivancanin once he got released. I was contemplating filing a private lawsuit against him for the damage that I sustained on account of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for you, Witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Olmsted, anything in redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, today you testified that -- that you believe that Mr. Milos Vojnovic sent you to Mrksic, to Colonel Mrksic, because none of the members of government had any contacts with them. First of all, can you tell us who did you mean when you said "them"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have information to the effect that any of the government members was in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's -- that's what I want to clarify. You're not -- you don't know the extent of government members' contacts with members of OG south. Is that what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness didn't say that. It is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a leading question, and the witness never said that he knows about the level of contacts, but he said that he doesn't know about contacts at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then let me rephrase it the way Defence counsel has suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of the level of contacts at all between government officials from SBWS and the OG south command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know about them having any contact, and I didn't have any information to the effect that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Defence counsel also asked you about your conversation with Mr. Hadzic on the 20th of November regarding the change from a military administration to a civilian administration. Just so we're very clear on the record, what specifically was discussed between you and Mr. Hadzic during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since a military administration was already in place, which meant that in the hospital there was a military physician who was the commander of the hospital, and I told Goran that I was in agreement with that, that civilian authorities should be brought in, that businesses should be revived because that would make it easier for Vuteks and Borovo to become operational again. Everything was destroyed. People were panic stricken as to how they would earn their livelihoods. There were no businesses. Nobody was farming the land. I was also of the view that civilian authorities should be introduced as soon as possible in order to restore life to Vukovar so that people would be able to make their earnings. We didn't have a single store in Vukovar. Everything was destroyed. There were no infirmaries. Since the army was there, the police could not discharge the duties that they would normally perform. That's why I was in agreement with him that it would have been better to have civilian authorities take over from the military administration as soon as may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to be clear, what did Mr. Hadzic suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only suggested that I should use my authority in order to have a civilian administration introduced as soon as possible, that I should work upon the army and that Rajko Bibic should be the president of the Executive Board and that he should be the one to put the government together. So he should be the prime minister-designate as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And to your knowledge did Mr. Bibic receive that appointment and become president of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you testified today that there was a military administration in Vukovar in placed for a couple of months. During this period what were the civilian authorities doing in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly. I only remember that when I formally took up my post within the transport company I co-operated with Mr. Crnogorac, who was minister for transport at the time. I didn't have any dealings with the others. With him I was in touch because I had to see to it that the transport company began work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you remember when that co-operation began?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was as soon as I took up my duty. The military administration was still in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just so we have a time-frame, when did you take up your duty with regard to this transportation company? How soon after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was several days later, I think. Workers who were there gathered and suggested that I be the manager and that we should turn former Cazmatrans into the Vukovar transport company. We immediately proceeded to find vehicles, to repair buildings. Those who were handymen went home to get tools to repair vehicles. I had pre-war acquaintances from whom I sought donations, and I managed to put together as many as 32 vehicles and put the company on its feet. It was quite successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jaksic. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, I have a couple of questions. The first question, it's about the six trailers that you mentioned today. What exactly happened with this -- these six trailers, the humanitarian aid trailers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These six trailer trucks carried humanitarian aid in the form of food and clothing for the civilian population of Vukovar. Subsequently, I heard that these goods were seen to be sold in the marketplace, so once more it was being sold to the civilians and somebody gained profit from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. And there was no proceeding, legal proceeding, against that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time. I don't know about the later period. Well, as far as I remember, the Court never initiated any proceedings for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Second question: On page 50 of the transcript yesterday, you talked about Vojnovic's wish to try Croats who were responsible for war crimes or those who had blood in their hands to be judged in the district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. My question is the following: Throughout all these events during the war, was there any trial organised at the district level to judge one of these Croats who was responsible for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A trial was held over there in Serbia, because this was at the time when Yugoslavia existed. It is common knowledge as to who among them received long-term sentences, who were the ones who participated in massacres. They were convicted. When Milan Panic became prime minister, he made this humanitarian gesture of handing them over to Serbia. So they never served their sentences either in Serbia or Croatia. In fact, they never were held to account for their crimes, and those Serbs who committed crimes in Croatia, they were handed over by Croatia to Serbia on condition that they do serve their sentences in Serbian prisons. When these persons who were convicted were handed over, Glavas received them, and he spoke openly in front of TV cameras, and he said, "Now are you free to be the Ustashas." And we knew who the Ustashas were. They were the ones who committed the worst acts, the acts of genocide during World War II, genocide against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back home. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've just been informed that now the next witness -- she was originally intended to be here in the building at 11.00, but we finished a little bit earlier than anticipated. They're bringing her now at 10.30, so if I could suggest we just take our break now and start at 11.00, which is the usual time. I think the witness will be ready to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll do that, Mr. Stringer. Court adjourned. We'll be back at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I do have a preliminary before the next witness is brought in, and it concerns the exhibits that are both associated or attached with the witness's 92 ter statement and other exhibits that may be tendered in the course of the examination by the Prosecution. A large number of these exhibits are not translated into B/C/S, and these exhibits are for the most part short documents. They are reports written by the witness or by others to other individuals inside UNPROFOR or within the United Nations. Now, my understanding of the case law is that once an exhibit is intended to be admitted, once it will be admitted as evidence, then it must be translated for the accused, and I can say that he has not had the opportunity to review a great many of the documents that will now be tendered with this witness's statement and her testimony. So to a large extent the prejudice has already been suffered and we'll have to live with that. As a remedy at this point, Mr. President, and I know you're always anxious to ask me, Well, what should be done, I would suggest that at a minimum none of the documents for which there is no B/C/S translation should be admitted at this stage, and they can be tendered at a later stage, including with reference to what may have been said by the witness, but at least for the time being we would request that none of these documents that do not have a B/C/S translation be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could take this one. I'm looking and I'm not finding the e-mail exchange that occurred between the parties and Chambers last September before the trial started. At that time, the Chamber instructed the parties that all documents in B/C/S had to be translated into English and up on e-court. We specifically raised the question at that time, given the competing -- excuse me, competing resource issues relating to translated documents. The Prosecution expressly asked the Chamber's guidance at that time whether the Prosecution would be obligated to obtain B/C/S translations of English documents. With a couple more minutes I can find the e-mail exchange in which the Chamber informed the parties that that was not the case, and that has never been -- it's been questioned on occasion, I think from the Defence, but the objections that have just been raised now certainly have not been raised with us with respect to any of the exhibits that are on the list for this witness. This is something that I don't believe counsel has indicated he intended to raise. But in any event, this goes back to the days before the trial, and we have not obtained translations into B/C/S of the documents because we're not required to. I think it bears noting on the record that from our observation the accused does seem to have the capability to communicate in English, and before we go about considering whether we're going to change the rules at this very late stage in the Prosecution case on preparation of translations, if the Chamber's minded to change the rules at this late phase, I think we're entitled to know really whether the accused is completely unable to read the documents or is he able to read them to some extent. Certainly he communicates with his counsel in English. It's a resource issue and if the Chamber is inclined to change the rules which we oppose and, in fact, at this late stage we're not going to be able to get translations done in the way and within the time-frame that's proposed now. Is it really necessary? That's question number two. Our issue -- response number two, I should say, issue. Response number one is it's not a requirement. It was expressly made not to be a requirement prior to the beginning of the trial after the issue was expressly raised by the Prosecution. We're a bit blind-sided by it now, and we most strongly would resist the Chamber changing the rules that it's laid out at the beginning. And just for the record, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're looking for the e-mail now, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. It's an e-mail received from the Chamber's Legal Officer on the 18th of September this year -- sorry, last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I didn't have the date nor the e-mail in front of me yet, but, Mr. Gosnell, you must know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Briefly in respond to those comments, Mr. President. Number one, we did raise this matter at the beginning of the trial. We did say that we expected exhibits that were actually going to be tendered to be translated into B/C/S. Thus far, it has not been a very significant problem because at least based on my interaction with the exhibits most of them have ultimately been translated, and as you may know, Your Honours, that's done on a rolling basis, and those are then uploaded to e-court and then they're provided in that way. What we're dealing with here is a very, very -- an exceptionally large number of documents that have not been translated and that is the difference between this and what has gone on in the past. In terms of Mr. Hadzic's ability, he can deal with short documents and there's no disagreement with about that, and I can state that for the record. But if you're dealing with anything that becomes complicated or lengthy he cannot handle that, he cannot understand that adequately, and I cannot consult with him adequately when it comes to longer documents and certainly in respect of the volume involved here. And finally, Mr. President, I'm only making an application in respect of this witness at this time because that's where we have a problem. The numbers are very significant in terms of this witness, in terms of the documents that have not been translated. And one caveat as well is my understanding of the case law is that translations are not required for public United Nations documents, so lengthy reports, resolutions and so forth. In previous cases that has not been required, but when you're dealing with internal correspondence reporting to be contemporaneous accounts of facts on the ground, that's important evidence, and it ought to be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In spite of the guidelines we gave in the 18 September e-mail, Mr. Gosnell, and if so, I'm a little bit surprised by your timing. If this is such a huge problem for this witness because of the volume of documents, shouldn't you have given the Trial Chamber and the OTP notice of your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. It's not the most timely objection, Mr. President, that's true. It should have -- it should have been brought last week when we became aware of the problem, and I regret that, and if Your Honours are minded to dismiss this application on the basis that it's untimely, then of course we'll accept that. If I could just have a moment, Mr. President, to look at the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm doing the same right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I do see that, and I suppose we're bound by that instruction. So I will -- I will withdraw that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I can quickly make an appearance, Your Honours. Lisa Biersay, on behalf of the Prosecution, and I am being assisted by our intern, Simona Onicel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Good -- no, it's still morning. Good morning, Mrs. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Blandina Francis Negga, and I was born on the 25th of September, 1933.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are about to make the solemn declaration, madam, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Can I now ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Negga. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we begin, I have conferred with the Defence regarding giving Mrs. Negga some hard copies because she does have some difficulties viewing documents on the screen because of her recent surgery. If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Negga.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we begin by asking you, can you hear me okay?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And are you comfortably seated?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That chair is a one-size fits all, I'm afraid. Okay. Thank you. Mrs. Negga, could you tell the Trial Chamber where you were born?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I was born in Barbuda, British West Indies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, what position did you hold from approximately May 1992 to August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I was a civil affairs co-ordinator for UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In which sector were you?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I was in Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, could you -- the Trial Chamber has heard evidence about Sector East, so could you just very briefly geographically describe where that sector was?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Sector East was a part of Croatia which borders on the Danube, and it includes such townships as Vukovar, Ilok, Beli Manastir in the north on the Hungarian border, and, of course, Osijek, which was the Croatian territory on another part outside the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you use the term "confrontation line," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Well, there was fighting in the former Yugoslavia, in -- specifically in Eastern Slavonia, and there is a line between Osijek in Croatia and the settled territory -- the territory settled by the Serbs, which was made -- which came to be known as the United Nations protected area or Sector East, and between those areas you had confrontation lines where there were mined areas and difficult territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in this Sector East, what were your primary duties?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Well, I was a political officer, and I co-ordinated the work of the military, the civilian police, and the civil affairs administration. My main problem -- my main task was to ensure the implementation of the Vance Plan and to have all the UN units working together, because we did work with the ICRC and UNHCR and other entities, and we were supposed to bring the Croats and the Serbs together to determine how they will decide to leave in peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Negga, on a day-to-day basis while you were the civil affairs co-ordinator in Sector East, what occupied most of your time?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Most of my time was occupied by the complaints of the minority groups in the area who wanted relief, respite, or just the chance to escape into -- into the Croatian occupied part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And from what did they seek relief and respite or a chance to escape?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Well, the minorities, mainly the Croats, Slovaks, Romans, they were being driven out of the area to make room for the incoming refugees from other parts of the former Yugoslavia, mainly from Bosnia-Herzegovina and other areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And these refugees, were they -- the ones coming in, were they Croats, Slovaks or Romanians that were all coming in?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No, they were all Serbs. They were all Serbs coming in.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would like to now direct your attention to June 2012. In June 2012, did you sign a statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now may I please ask the Registrar to display the English original of 65 ter number 2794, which is tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you have that in your binder, I believe, Mrs. Negga. And it's dated 7 June 2012. And if possible, if we could go directly to page 4, B/C/S page 4. And for you, Mrs. Negga, it would be simply marked as page 1 at the bottom where there is your name --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- and date of birth. If we could also in the English go to page -- page 4 in the English. Thank you. Mrs. Negga, do you recognise this page?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It's my witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the signatures at the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, my own signature, Blandina Francis Negga.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you subsequently initial the pages thereafter?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, when you prepared and signed your statement in June 20 -- excuse me, 2012, were certain documents referenced in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you also reviewed those; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could now go to the very first page of the document. And, Mrs. Negga, after you reviewed and signed your statement, did you meet with a representative from the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did the representative certify your statement?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the very first page of the entire exhibit. Thank you. And directing your attention to this page, do you recognise this page as well that we're looking at, which is the very first page. Not the first page of your statement, but the part where the certification by the Registrar. So if you flip to the beginning, one more --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: "Declaration by a person making a written."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you signed a certification attesting to the truthfulness of your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in preparation for your appearance today, have you had an opportunity to read and review your 2012 statement?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you reviewed it, did you find some items that you wanted to modify?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I found two minor, but they were more editorial than factual.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we could look at paragraph 113, which is -- I believe, in e-court it will be page 25 in the English, but for you, Mrs. Negga, it will be page 21 that will be written at the bottom of your -- of your statement. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm now directing your attention to the second to last sentence in paragraph 113?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what in that sentence, if anything, would you like to -- to strike?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I would like to strike after the penultimate line "RSK." I would like to strike the rest of the sentence and just put a full stop after "RSK." Because the sentence goes on to read -- the whole sentence says: "I heard about legislation granting RSK citizenship to persons of Serbian nationality residing outside the RSK, was familiar with some discriminatory RSK legislation such as." I am not familiar with the legislation nor can I recall having seen such legislation. So I suggest that you end the sentence at the second RSK in that -- in that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Negga. And I believe the next one that you had referred to was on page 24 for you, Mrs. Negga.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For the Registry it would be page 28, and it would be in paragraph 137. And again it would be the second line from the bottom and it says "other at in," and if I'm correct you wanted to strike the word "at."

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, with these corrections made, is the statement truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just verifying one matter. So, Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 2794 as well as the associated exhibits listed in tabs 1 through 71 of the exhibit list that was forwarded to the Defence and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, Mr. President. I think there's one more question that needs to be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One more [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ms. Negga, if you were asked the same questions today would you in substance give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And at this time I would resubmit for admission 65 ter number 2794 and its associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement will become Exhibit P2398, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Negga, in paragraph 85 of your statement, which is on page 16, you discuss Arkan's Tigers being seen in the sector armed with long weapons. And in your statement you describe that these very weapons were forbidden under the Vance Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to, if we could, go to 65 ter number 5250, which should be tab 119.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that should also be in your -- in your binder. And for the record, this is dated 16 September 1992, and it's described as an UNPROFOR UNCIVPOL headquarter Sector East report from Larry W. Moore entitled: "Minutes of meeting with Baranja authorities on 16 September 1992." Now, Mrs. Negga, if you could go to the -- and also with the Registry if we could go to page 3, which is the last page of the document. Go to the very bottom. At the bottom there are the initials L.W. and the last name Moore. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who is it?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Larry Moore was the deputy civil police monitor in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And during the course of your tenure, would you receive reports and briefings from him?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention back to the first page, I'd like to look at the second paragraph listing the attendees, and it lists UNPROFOR representatives as Colonel Jockin, Mrs. Negga, Corwin, Maldeghem, Sergeant Moore. Do you recognise those names?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, of course there is your name. Who is Colonel Jockin?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Colonel Jockin was the head of the Belgian battalion that was stationed in Beli Manastir on the Hungarian border.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the reference to Sergeant Moore, is that reference to?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: To Larry Moore of CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, it described as well local authorities were represented by Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Latas, and Mr. Vranac and three other men. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recall this meeting held on September 16th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why is it that you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It was somewhat vituperous because Mr. Zivanovic felt that UNPROFOR was unfriendly towards the Serbs and the meeting ended in disarray.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And regarding that, if I could direct you to the discussion regarding Mr. Zivanovic and it's the last -- the beginning of the last paragraph where it reads Mr. Zivanovic - you see that? - and it's on page 1 of the document if you go back.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And towards the bottom of the page it says: Mr. Zivanovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And specifically I wanted to look at number 1 that summarises what Mr. Zivanovic had to say. He said: "UNPROFOR had lost the trust of the Serbian people and the local authorities because it did not choose to fulfil its humanitarian mandate." Is that what you were referring to when you described Mr. Zivanovic's view regarding UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And turning to the next page, looking at number 4 it says -- it receipts: "Today, the Baranja has given its reply as to the return of the refugees." What was the -- the reply regarding the return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: The -- it was determined that the time was not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the return for which refugees?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: The -- the Croatians who had been living in the area and the other minority groups who had been living in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And underneath number 5, "He," presumably Mr. Zivanovic, "informed us that he will go on radio Beli Manastir to report the above to the public." Do you recall that from the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 5 that I skipped, Mr. Zivanovic's position was that UNPROFOR had tried to use blackmailing tactics to arrange a meeting between authorities on both sides of the conflict. Do you -- do you remember that allegation?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was your response regarding that allegation?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I dismissed it, because our function there was to bring the two sides together to discuss how they will get over the -- they would get beyond what had happened and just how they would decide to live together in peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in the second full paragraph from the end that reads, "Thereupon, Mr. Zivanovic." I'd like to focus on the last sentence in that paragraph which connects to the paragraph we looked at in your statement about disarming. And Mr. Zivanovic stated that just as UNPROFOR was bound by its instructions, he could not discuss demilitarisation until he received instructions from Knin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did you understand him to mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I understood that they got directions from above, and they couldn't exercise initiative, and they had to wait to be told what to say and how to react to our proposals.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Towards the end of this report, Moore describes what could be expected as consequences based on the content of this meeting, and I'd like to focus your attention on number 1 where he writes: "There will probably be an increase in terrorist activities and in anti-UNPROFOR back-lash since the proposed radio interview could be used as a means of inciting the population." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And then I'd like to look at number 2, which is on the next page, and again focusing on the disarming process it reads: "There could well be another further deadlock in the disarming process continues it is claimed that the instructions must be received from Knin." What was your experience after this meeting regarding the disarming process within Sector East?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite get that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did disarming proceed as provided under the Vance Plan after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time we would tender 65 ter number 5250.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2399, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 28 of your statement, you describe that quickly your main focus became to prevent further ethnic cleansing across the sector, and you defined what you understood to be ethnic cleansing, which is to mean riding an area of all people so that one group remains. In this case, Serbs were to be the sole remaining group in the area. Do you recall that from your statement?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, if we could take a look, please, at 65 ter number 1279, which should be tab 153, dated 27 September 1992, a press article entitled: "Killing that makes Croatia fit for Serbs," published by "The Independent." And I'd first turn my attention to the very first paragraph under the word "Body." Do you have it, Ms. Negga? Can I assist?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It has the tab number 153 and it should be in sequential order. So probably at the very back. Oh, excuse me -- yes.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No, my last tab is 152.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. And I -- I'll -- I'll skip that one. If you take a look at the screen, are you able to read it or is it too difficult to read?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let's try.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. So we can even enlarge it further by -- there we go. And it reads: "This is now the land of the Serbian people. And so it will stay for the next 1.000 years. If the Croats do not like it, we will start a new war." And this is attributed to Borivoje Zivanovic, a Serb who was referring to Baranja. There was also a Zivanovic referenced in the document that we just looked at. Is this the same Zivanovic or a different Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I think it's the same Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the -- the second page, at the top. It reads: "Colonel Jean-Marie Jockin, the UN military chief in Baranja said, 'Terrorists activities are going on. This means shooting people, beating, torture, and robbery.'" And you previously described who Mr. Jockin was. Was that your experience in Sector East regarding acts of what he calls terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At this stage I'm compelled to object. We're leading the witness too much, I think, at this point. The witness has eloquently set forth her testimony in her 92 ter statement, and she can answer questions here, but putting propositions from a newspaper article without knowing precisely the basis for the journalist's indication of this information I would suggest that that's leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The witness has described her experience in her statement, and she just described through a report the challenges being faced by UNPROFOR. And this is not leading. The question I asked called for a yes or no answer the way it was phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Towards the middle of the page, the paragraph that begins "Meanwhile." It describes an elderly Croatian couple being killed, and it reads: "'Mr. Andric had his guts cut out and his wife had her head blown off,' Blandina, a UN civil affairs coordinator in eastern Croatia ..." is that quote correctly attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it goes on to say that you describe the high level of terrorism in UN zones adding that: "99 per cent of the victims were non-Serbs. The pattern is threats followed by bombings, followed by killing." Again, is that quote properly attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did that pattern exist throughout your tenure in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes. It was replicated in other villages and other areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now directing your -- your attention to the last paragraph where it begins "Ms. Negga": "Ms. Negga linked the rise in terrorism to the busing into Baranja, mostly [sic] by night, of thousands of Serbian refugees from Bosnia and other parts of Croatia." Is that information properly attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And was it accurate?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time we would tender 65 ter number 1279 for admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2400.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to -- let's see if this is in your binder, Mrs. Negga. Tab -- do you have tab 123?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for the Registry, that's 65 ter number 5260. It's dated 28 September 1992, an UNPROFOR letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 120 in your statement, you describe that life had become simply so unbearable for non-Serbs that they -- they had to leave, and I'd like to address that in the context of this exhibit.
