If we could please go to the second page first, because it's dated before the first page. Oh, forgive me. The third page. Do you have the page, the letter that begins "Dear Mrs. Negga"? I think that's --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No, I don't. I have my reply, but not --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you -- could we just check to see -- or if I could get the binder back, perhaps I can find the missing document. If I could have some assistance. Could we enlarge the -- the section that reads "Dear Mrs. Negga." If we -- could we make it just a little bit smaller, and I will show the heading to Mrs. Negga. And it's addressed to you, Mrs. Blandina Francis Negga, and it's from Mr. Milan Ilic, president of Regional Council, and it's written at the top that it's the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you recall this letter that he sent to you?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go down to the first paragraph, and I'll -- I'll read it slowly. It reads: "According to our talks we had in Regional Council on 21st of September concerning transfer of some seven people from the settlement of Svinjarevci," I'm sure you have better pronunciation, Ms. Negga, "I must inform you that I sent a letter immediately to our internal affairs office in Vukovar, asking them to issue a permission that those people in question can leave this territory and go to the other (Croatian) side." Could you give us some context for that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: This village of Svinjarevci they were all the people continually harassed, threatened, and physically handled, and they wished to go over to Osijek to escape that type of treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now if I could move to the third paragraph. Again Mr. Ilic continues saying: "The internal affair officer promised me that this very day they receive such request from those people. They are going to issue a permission for them to leave this territory and go to Croatian side." And in response to that you sent a letter to Mr. Ilic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that would be the very first page of the document. And I do have a hard copy of that. If we could just assist Mrs. Negga's eyes a bit. Thank you. And I would like to focus on the -- I'd like to focus on the paragraph that begins "Although": You wrote: "Although I can understand that in normal situations one must file an application with the internal affairs office in Vukovar for permission to leave the territory in order to ensure safe return in future, your request in this instance seems cynical and unjustified. It would be a cruel hoax to pretend that these unfortunate people were leaving their homes and their community voluntarily. "Quite simply, it would be a lie." What was the basis for your characterisation?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Well, the practice was that anyone who left the territory voluntarily would have their property immediately confiscated. Those who wanted to return would have to prove that they were not consorting with the Croatian side and that they were loyal to the Serbian side. In my opinion, the repeated efforts to push people over the border was mainly to confiscate their property and make those properties available to the incoming refugees, and I thought that they wanted UNPROFOR to somehow collude in this matter, and I just couldn't, and that is why I wrote this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And -- and at this time we move for the admission of 65 ter number 5260.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2401.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, again picking up on the -- the words you wrote in the statement regarding ethnic cleansing, I'd like to look at 65 ter number 1272, which may be in your -- in your binder. If we could just have some assistance from the -- assistance from the Registry in checking the binder for that, and in the meantime, if we could please turn to 65 ter number 1272, tab 75. And that is dated 22 September, 1992, a press article entitled: "Non-Serbs killed as ethnic cleansing surges in Croatia," published by "The Guardian" on that date. Now, I'd like to go down to the paragraph which I think is the fourth one that begins "Blandina Negga." It references you as the UN civil affairs co-ordinator for the eastern region, and it's: "According to this, Blandina Negga said that while the scale of the Bosnian refugee influx had yet to be established, the ethnic cleansing programme had been carefully planned. She admitted that the UN forces authorised to administer the area under last January's UN peace plan were powerless to prevent the resettlement." Mrs. Negga, is that information accurately attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is the information correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what was your basis for concluding that the US -- the UN peace plan was powerless to prevent the resettlement?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: The UN forces were sent in to stand between the Croatians and the Serbs. They were not there to perform any local services. They -- for example, the civilian police could not apprehend or administer justice. They were there to monitor the local police, to draw any -- any -- anything that was out of the ordinary to their attention and to advise them how situations could be corrected. They could not themselves initiate action to prevent any upcoming settlement or whatnot. They were just there to advise and not to act.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And along those lines was UNPROFOR permitted to prosecute crimes?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: They were not. They were only there to draw to the attention of the police and the prosecutor what was happening and to monitor their actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now directing your attention to the next paragraph in which you're again quoted. You describe it as: "'It's very organised,' she said. 'They're given houses by the local authorities or put up as guests in the homes of non-Serbs who end up leaving in most instances. It's not part of our mandate to stop refugees coming into the area. Virtually all of the houses abandoned by Croats during the war were now inhabited,' she added." Is that information correctly attributed to you?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is it correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time, we tender 65 ter 1272.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2402, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, hopefully you have tab 36, so it should be before the document. Could we have some assistance in identifying tab 36 for Mrs. Negga. And that is 65 ter number 5241. Could we please have displayed on e-court 5241.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, Mrs. Negga, at paragraphs 40, 41, and 42, you describe a meeting, a September 4 meeting, September 4 1992 meeting with Knin authorities including Goran Hadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And this is referenced in your statement, and if I could direct your attention to the screen, Mrs. Negga. Are you able to see it?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If not, we can print a copy upstairs and bring it in to you. Are you able to see it?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. And it's dated -- this document is dated 5 September 1992, and it is and UNPROFOR Sector East telefax, and subject: Summary of meeting with Knin authorities. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is from Heather Felsinger to Cedric Thornberry. Who is Heather Felsinger?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: She was first my secretary and then later civil affairs officer in Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you present for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And directing your attention to the -- the second page. But before we get there, generally what was the purpose of Heather Felsinger sending this document to Cedric Thornberry?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It was for the record of what transpired.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if we could zoom in on the first half. It describes Mr. Marrack Goulding, Under-Secretary-General for peacekeeping operations, opening the meeting? Do you recall him being present?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the next paragraph it references Mr. Hadzic speaking on behalf the Knin authorities. Do you recall Mr. Hadzic being present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And according to this report Mr. Hadzic speaking on behalf of the Knin authorities said that the main purpose of their attendance at the meeting today, being the 4th of September, 1992, was hopefully to remove one step further in ending the war and bringing about peace to the Serbian people. Is that what's reflected in that document?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go to the next paragraph that begins "In reply": "In reply, Mr. Goulding thanked Mr. Hadzic for his expression that the United Nations could assist in bringing about an end to the war and that Krajina accepted the Vance Plan. He stated, however, that such a statement did not reflect the actual situation in Sector East." Do you recall that exchange at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Based on what Mr. Hadzic said, was it -- how did you view the statement and whether it reflected the actual situation in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was Mr. Goulding's view that the expression that Mr. Hadzic had made about the United Nations assisting in bringing an end to the war, and the statement that the Krajina accepted the Vance Plan, Mr. Goulding said that such a statement by Hadzic did not reflect the actual situation in Sector East. Did you agree with Mr. Goulding or did you disagree with him.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. Goulding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why did you agree with him?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Because there was lawlessness in Sector East, and there was no discernible advance to any peace or any discussing how a peace would be achieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to go further in that paragraph which is about halfway, and it begins on the right-hand side: "UNPAs had not been completely demilitarised. The multipurpose police brigades and milicija with long weapons continued to parade in the sector. These forces knew nothing about police work. They have no discipline and behave as terrorists, not as soldiers." Did you agree or disagree with that characterisation by Mr. Goulding?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I agreed completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to the next page. One would be -- and focus on the second paragraph. And this begins "Mr. Kadzic." In your statement you indicated that that was incorrect. It should read "Mr. Hadzic"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "And Mr. Kadzic," Hadzic, "asked how his local authorities could demilitarise the territory when the Serbian people were under constant threat by the Croatians. He stated that he was ashamed that the Vance Plan was not being implemented." Now, halfway down the page in the same paragraph, the sentence under the number "10.000 Serbs." If you go down two more lines and that's a sentence that begins, "With respect to ethnic cleansing." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "With respect to ethnic cleansing, he," Mr. Hadzic, "stated that the Croatians started this practice in Western Slavonia prior to any practice followed by the Serbs." And he continues that: "They organised meetings and ordered all the Serbs to leave the region. During the war they killed women and children without mercy. Such events led to our belief ... we should act 'for an eye and tooth for a tooth.' At present, we could stop ethnic cleansing and death sentences could be exercised against those who transgressed." Do you recall that from the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, according to this in the next paragraph Mr. Goulding replied and he reiterated his belief that ethnic cleansing continued to be practiced and that such cases were well documented by UNPROFOR CIVPOL: "He noted the return of 10.000 Serbs to Western Slavonia could under no circumstances precede the return of the refugees from Croatia to Serbia to their homes." Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, this is part of the 92 ter package but at this time the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 5241.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I must admit I do not really understand what you are asking, Ms. Biersay. It's part of the package?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is part of the package. I know it's been -- the practice has gone both ways. Sometimes we defer it to be given a number with all the others, and sometimes we admit them if the Prosecution deals with it in the courtroom. And I was proposing to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If it's part of the package it will be admitted --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- in the package in that manner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if I could please have displayed 65 ter number 6463. Which is tab 152.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I see that you have this in your folder, Mrs. Negga.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, it's the handwritten notes that I took during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could we please go to the next page. And is this also part of the same notes about the meeting on the 4th September 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, please. And this is a continuation?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we now go to the very last page, please. I don't know if it's possible to rotate. This is entitled: "Meeting with Knin authority." What is this that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It's a chart of the seating arrangement for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And these are the attendees who were actually at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time we would tender 65 ter number 6463.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2403, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock, and I'm happy to continue, but I'm moving to another document and thought perhaps this would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, Ms. Biersay. Thank you very much. Mrs. Negga, this is the time for the Trial Chamber's second break. We'll take 30 minutes and come back at 12.45. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we have a minute, I would like to make -- renew or modify my previous application and that is to request that any of the associated exhibits with this witness's statement be translated into B/C/S. I'm not requesting that it be a condition of admission. I'm simply asking that that be required. And I realise that perhaps written submissions will be required, but maybe not, so I thought I would just put it on the record and see if we could save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is there a position already?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Defence is free to request that of CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, would that be the course of action that can be taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Happy to do it that way. We'll make the request, and if there's a large back-log, we'll come back to the Chamber on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Negga, hopefully opened in front of you is tab 115, which is for our record 65 ter number 5234. Do you have something marked as tab 115?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Very good. And it's dated 2 September 1992. And if we could please have that displayed on the screen. And while that is appearing on the screen, Mrs. Negga, I'd like to make reference to paragraph 38 of your statement, which reads: "I recall one episode that showed the level of control RSK authorities had on the ground. One day I was stopped on the way to Osijek by the RSK Special Police patrolling the no man's land, a mined area between Erdut and Osijek. They demand our papers. I insisted that I was with the UN and I refused to provide the requested papers. Several hours passed, and eventually General Kromchenkov, head of the Russian battalion" -- shall we take a little pause, Mrs. Negga?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No. That's all right. I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay: "Kromchenkov, the head of the Russian battalion of UNPROFOR called Milan Milanovic who called off these border police." And this is in your statement. And it is in that regard I'd like to look at this document, and, first of all, it is from you; is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And to Yolanda Auger, do I pronounce that correctly?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to move to the next page. And at the bottom again there is the name L.W. Moore. That's the same person we discussed earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, this document refers to the missing persons from Sector East, and specifically it -- you received information that there were perhaps prisoner camps in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, regarding that, if you look at the second paragraph from the bottom it begins "This office," and it reads: "This office cannot dispute that there were prisoner camps in this area either during or after the war. We cannot even state for certain that no camps exist now. There are still several sites controlled by paramilitary or Special Police groups within the UNPA where neither CIVPOL or UNMO have access." Was that consistent with the Vance Plan that neither CIVPOL nor UNMO would have access to sites on -- sites in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you've had an opportunity to review this entire document previously; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it's accurate as far as the information you received?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time we'd tender into evidence 65 ter number 5234.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mrs. Negga?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The document is marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2404, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if we could please have displayed 65 ter number 5210.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Negga, this should be tab 108. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excellent. It's dated 17 July 1992. Now, this relates to paragraphs 81 to 82 of your statement where you discussed perpetrators, and paragraph 30, where perpetrators threatened a Croatian man that if he did not leave Dalj he would be killed the next day. So I'd like to now turn your attention to this document, and it is from Kjell Johansen to Cedric Thornberry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, the second sentence reads: "This report gives the background for the action that has taken place either by CAC, Mrs. Negga, Sector East, or myself." And the person writing this report is Mr. Hansen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Mr. Johansen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Johansen. Thank you. Now, do you recall this incident described in the report regarding Doko Briga?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph there is a discussion about the description of the meeting opening. Johansen describes giving a short presentation about observation, and that he visited the oldest of two Croatian men in his house on 8 July 1992. And he was advised in the presence of Gerard Sexton and Sergeant Larry Moore that the previous night this Croatian man was visited by Doko Briga in his home and beaten severely. And he writes: "The man was lying in his bed with great pain, showed me his bleeding feet, legs and back. He could hardly move." And then the next line it describes that the man had known Doko Briga for years. Is that consistent with the information that you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, this goes on to describe in that last paragraph that the chief of police made a long statement and said that there was no legal cause to force and arrest Doko Briga because this was a quarrel. Do you recall him telling you that at the time?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And according to this report, you replied, "If you are applying such laws, your laws are barbaric." Did you make that comment?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why did you make that comment?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Because when you looked at the man, how badly he was beaten, you know, you couldn't help but wonder why, and ordinary fights between people were not that bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you previously reviewed this document. Does it accurately reflect the information regarding the meeting and information that you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 5210.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2405.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Negga, do you have marked in your binder 109?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 37 of your statement, you state: "I believe that the refusal of the local police to investigate or prevent crimes against non-Serbs came as a policy directly from the RSK government. In fact, shortly after arriving in the sector, I noted that the local police were either participants in these beatings and expulsions or stood idly by while these crimes occurred." And I'd like to direct your attention to 65 ter number 5214, which is tab 109, and it's dated 22 July 1992. And looking at the first page of that document. It's from Mohamed Abdul Aziz, civil affairs officers Beli Manastir, to Cedric Thornberry. Who was Mr. Abdul Aziz?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: He was also an officer in UNPROFOR, and when I travelled, he replaced me as the acting civil affairs administrator in Erdut, or he was stationed in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I note that there's a CC at the bottom of this document, CC Blandina Negga?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the contents of this report?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It is a long handwritten report, and I'd just like to focus on a few aspects of it. And this will be the last document that I discuss with you. If I could direct your attention to the third page. Number 3. And if we can -- it we could try to enlarge it. And it's up to you, Mrs. Negga, if you find it more useful to look at the screen or the paper, but I'd like to -- the sixth line down towards the right it starts, "Fugitives from justice." Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it reads: "Fugitives from justice are perceived by some of the local leaders and military and police commanders as heroes. Serious criminals are being released from prison a few days after their arrest. Even at times when the local police does its work professionally, the result of their efforts is frustrated by irresponsible decisions of the Judges who act under the constant pressure of the political leaders who interfere [sic] in releasing terrorists." How does that compare with your experience and the information that you had in Sector East during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: That is exactly what happened. He described the situation clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in 4 he continues on and he discusses some things you've already discussed, so I won't go over that. Briefly, he references that all individuals and families who collaborated with the enemy and so forth are not permitted inside of Baranja. What I'd like to do is to skip to the point 5 that's there. And the first sentence reads: "The process of ethnic cleansing is not only conducted by way of terrorising the population and use of threats but also by using economic pressure." Is that statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you briefly describe to the Trial Chamber what economic pressure was put on non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Non-Serbs were dismissed from jobs that they had held for years, some over 20 years, and they were just laid off, and they had no other means of existing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we would tender 65 ter 5214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before that, Ms. Biersay, in the line just before 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You read the verb in that line as "interfere." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Negga, how do you read that word?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It says "who intervene."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "Intervene in releasing terrorists."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2406, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, this concludes the Prosecution's direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Sorry for the delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Negga. Am I correct in addressing you as Mrs. Negga or is it Ms. Negga?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: "Missus" would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you for that. My name is Christopher Gosnell, and I represent Mr. Hadzic, and I'll be asking you a few questions today and tomorrow. If anything I do ask you isn't clear, please feel free to ask me to elaborate and I'll try to my best. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: During the 14 months that you were in Sector East, which I understand was approximately between June 1992 and August 1993, do I understand correctly that you met Mr. Hadzic once?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I recall that meeting vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That was the only face-to-face meeting you had with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: As I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that meeting that you attended was also attended by Under-Secretary-General Marrack Goulding and the civil affairs chief Cedric Thornberry for UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were the principal interlocutors, the people who were speaking to one another at the meeting, Mr. Goulding on the one side and then various ministers on the RSK side?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It was mainly Mr. Hadzic, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You don't recall Mr. Martic --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- addressing the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, he did. According to my notes he did address the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that meetings with Mr. Hadzic as president of the RSK, to use an expression, would have been above your pay grade? What I mean to say by that is that you would not have one-to-one meeting with Mr. Hadzic as --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- civil affairs co-ordinator for Sector East. Meetings with Mr. Hadzic would be carried out either by Mr. Goulding or Mr. Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You testified earlier about some notes that were prepared by Ms. Felsinger, I believe, and in those notes there's an indication that Mr. Hadzic used the expression: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. Can you please tell us what was the context of that particular statement, and what precisely did you understand him to be saying?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I understand that whatever the Croatians did against the Serbs would be met with similar fashion. You know, a eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. And those were words that were telling, because in a meeting when you hear those words you perk up when you hear them, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: These for you that would be a noteworthy declaration, wouldn't it, by a president of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Noteworthy in what respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Important.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Important, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you understand that he was advocating that position, or did you understand that he was describing what was occurring on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: The latter. I got the impression he was saying that whatever they did, we will retaliate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure your answer is entirely clear. Let me try to pose it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The -- the answer was very clear. It may not be one which counsel likes, but it's very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is in my understanding a little confusion in there, Ms. Biersay. I'll overrule the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's go back to your answer. You said the latter, and the latter concerned events as they were occurring on the ground. Was that what you intended to say when you said the latter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Gosnell, it would be fair to the witness to repeat the question as you put the question to the witness. Now that her attention is gone to the latter and the former, I think we will get a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mrs. Negga, let me try again putting the question. The question that I asked was: Did you understand that he was advocating that position, or did you understand that he was describing what was occurring on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I'd say neither. I got the impression that he's saying, Whatever they do, we will retaliate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that mean you're suggesting he was advocating an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yeah. If he says, If you do this, then we will follow through, and we will reply in kind. So if you think that is advocating, then I think it's up to you, but this is what I understood, Should you do this, we will retaliate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: To my mind there is a distinction, a possible distinction, between advocating as a matter of RSK policy on the one side and describing, on the other hand, what is occurring. What I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I think that the question is asked and answered now. Don't you think so?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I -- there has been an answer in some way, but I believe I could explore it further without being repetitive, because I'm not sure that all the dimensions of the question or the answer have been explored and it is an important issue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Biersay, you want to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness has been very clear about it, and it is asked and answered, and I think I count at least -- it's been asked and answered at least three times according to my count, and I believe it's been answered and Defence counsel should be asked to -- to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'll give you one more -- one last chance, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was he using this -- was he using that expression to explain to Mr. Goulding what he believed was occurring, not as a matter of government policy but what bandits, extremists, uncontrolled elements, were doing in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's exactly a repeat of the questions with a new tinge to it in an effort to, I think, have the witness modify her previous answer that she's given three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 06463, please, which was a document used by the Prosecution, and the tab number is --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could assist --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- 152. And it might be best to have the typewritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly, Mrs. Negga, that you reviewed these handwritten notes, and you attempted to transcribe in typewritten form what you had written in your handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we go down there to the penultimate paragraph on page 1, you describe an intervention by Mr. Hadzic, and there's that section beginning: "In the manner -- matter of ethnic cleansing, many mistakes were made starting in Western Slavonia by officials of the Croatian government. According to information, 170 villages were affected. He recalled the events of World War II. He boasted that Krajina was stronger than Croatia, which was a death sentence for the European Community." Now, there's no mention in your notes of Mr. Hadzic having declared that it was RSK policy to exchange an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Is there some reason why that wasn't included?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: There's no reason that I can remember after 20 years, but I heard those words, and to me I was just making a summary of what was said. I wasn't going into any great detail word by word.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That wasn't a shocking declaration to hear, that it was a matter of RSK policy to take revenge on a mass scale --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: After what had happened in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection. That's not what it stated, and this is a proposition that's being put by Mr. Gosnell and his reading of it and interpretation. So I believe that the actual phrase should be used in the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I am putting a proposition, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Was there a declaration that it was a matter of RSK policy to take revenge?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I thought that -- well, I thought at the end of the questions I had previously asked that that was the ultimate conclusion, unless I've badly misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The point, if I may, is that this statement that Mr. Gosnell -- or proposition or whatever he would like to call it, the fact that that proposition is not in her notes makes sense because that was never said, and she's explained that she summarised the information, but she -- there's no information anywhere that this specific proposition was uttered at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, if the Prosecution will stipulate to that, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I confess that I share the trouble alluded to by the President about the way that you phrase -- that you phrase the question. It seems that it is -- what the witness is being asked to take on board, as it were, is more than she herself would have spoken to in the notes to which she referred, so to that extent the question strikes me as being somewhat unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps I should break it down and proceed in steps to make it fair and more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's see where that will lead us, Mr. Gosnell. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me ask it this way: Did Mr. Goulding respond to this declaration?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I'd have to read -- I'd have to read Mr. Goulding's response as we summarised them, but I don't recall Mr. Goulding using "Eye for eye, tooth for tooth" in his response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, I wasn't suggesting that. I was just asking you whether you could recall what Mr. Goulding's response was, if any, to the use of those particular words.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: As I said, I don't recall him using those particular words.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say "him," are you referring --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Mr. Goulding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And regardless of whether he used those words or other words, can you recall whether he responded in any way to those words having been used?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As you sit here can you recall what Mr. Goulding said during the meeting? Without having regard to your notes.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Sir, it's over 20 years, huh, that I'm being asked to relive a horrific period of my life, huh. I'm suffering from PTSD, and you're asking me to recall word-for-word what somebody said when it's clearly stated in all the reports I wrote which were almost simultaneously reported as the incidents occurred? That is not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Negga, I think that you misunderstood Mr. Gosnell's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What he's asking you is whether you do recall the words or not. If you don't recall the words, nobody will blame you for that. It's just to know whether it is still in your memory right now or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With all due respect, sir, I have replied to that question over and over again. He asked me did Mr. Goulding, the Under-Secretary-General, reply to the tooth for tooth or eye for eye, and I said I don't recall him saying that. What more can I say? I answered his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So do we take it from that that you don't recall anymore what Mr. Goulding said at that moment, not particularly in reply to the tooth for a tooth phrase but in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. Mr. Goulding was refuting that the situation had advanced any -- much, because the situation in the sector had not improved, and Mr. Goulding went through a list of what was wrong and what hadn't progressed. I recall that clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I take it Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Hadzic was speaking in Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You don't speak Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The meeting was being interpreted by someone.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you have any sense of the quality of the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: We -- we had the best interpreters that were available, and that is my sense, that they were doing a good job.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I simply ask you that because not everyone agrees that all UN interpreters were of the utmost highest quality, and I simply wanted to ask you as a general matter whether there was anything in the manner of the interpretation that would cause you to doubt whether it was perfect and precise.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: There wasn't that I recall, and there were no objections made at the time, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you yourself were not speaking during this meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you attempt to make your notes that you prepared at the time as full and complete a record of the meeting as possible?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I always do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were you making those notes at the time, during the meeting, or did you make them afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of the notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Well, clearly they were made simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could go now to paragraph 53 of your statement. Here you say: "In early 1993, the RSK authorities communicated with the UN Secretary-General. I was sent a copy of the letter that Hadzic had written to the Secretary-General in which he emphasised the RSK's fears of an imminent Croatian attack. I thought this fear was unjustified because the Croatians were pushing me to arrange the return of the displaced Croats. I think it was very unlikely that the Croatians would have attacked the area to which they were trying to return displaced Croatians. It was Hadzic's form of propaganda." Now, I'd like to look at the letter that you're referring to in your footnote, and it's Prosecution tab 61, 05322. And am I correct, Mrs. Negga, that when you prepared this statement you were -- you had the documents to hand that you put in your footnotes?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The 65 ter number again is 05322.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is this indeed the letter that you meant to refer to as -- in that footnote?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether a hard copy might be available. I thank my colleague for that courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, there it says at the outset of this letter -- I'm sorry. Let me -- let me give you a chance to answer my question. Was this the document you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At the outset it says: "The Republic Serbian Krajina which has been established on the territories of former Yugoslavia, by the wish of their own people, is exposed to the permanent aggression of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia from 21 January 1993 until this time." Now, if we go to page 2: "At this moment we are exposed to the big number of refugees who are coming from the Benkovac area and numbering close to 10.000." Now, seeing that name Benkovac, does that help you recall what events may have been occurring at around this date?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I seem to be missing a page, so I don't quite follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could zoom in. It should be page 2. Yes, we're there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You don't have page 2 in your papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mrs. Negga, is that large enough?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "At this moment we are exposed to the big number of refugees who are coming from Benkovac area and numbering close to 10.000." Does that remind you of what events may have been ongoing at around this date? And the date of this letter is 30th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It says here that it was in western -- it was in Sector West, which adjoined Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not there yet. I'm just above that, Mrs. Negga. Do you see where -- can you see the name "Benkovac area"?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that name remind you as to whether there were any very significant events ongoing at around this date?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you remember as whether part of your functions in Sector East were you kept abreast of events in other sectors, security events in particular?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Periodically we received reports on each sector from the military command in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then now let's go to the next paragraph which you, I think, already read. It says: "Unfortunately, according to our knowledge, military forces of the Republic of Croatia are preparing themselves for further aggressive movements towards the territories of Western Slavonia (Sector West) which is planning in the next few days." Now, is that what you say is propaganda, Mr. Hadzic's propaganda?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I read that the threat was in Sector East, you know. I did not read Sector West threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All I'm trying to understand is you are saying that Mr. Hadzic, in this letter, is engaging in propaganda, and I'm just trying to understand why you believe he was engaging in propaganda. On what basis do you say that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: The Croats -- the Croats were urging Sector East to arrange for the return of the refugees, and to me, to suggest that they are -- they will be attacking the Serbs at the same time that they're waiting for the return of the refugees seemed to me somewhat incongruous, and that is why I used the term "propaganda."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you deemed the threat of an attack to be low or insignificant because the Croats, the Croatian side, wished to repopulate those areas?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes. In Sector East, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you see here that Mr. Hadzic is talking about the threat of an attack not on Sector East but in Sector West?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yeah, I see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Having seen that, would you retract that -- your statement that he is engaging in propaganda in this letter?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Insofar as it doesn't apply to Sector East, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 03170, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps before we lose this document I could just ask you one more question while it's nicely on the screen in front of us. It says further down in the last paragraph: "It is, unfortunately, obvious that we are forced to protect our people and territories by all military powers unless the Croatian aggression is not stopped." And just above that he says: "... as we have done several times in the past, we kindly ask you," and this letter is addressed to the president of the Security Council, "again to take necessary measures for preventions." Would you agree that what appears to be expressed here is a sincere, leaving aside whether it's legitimate, a sincere concern about the danger of a Croatian attack at this time?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: He's pleading for help, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He's pleading for help, and would you also agree he's also saying that, Unless we get that help, we have to protect ourselves?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Well, he says that in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Negga. Can we now please go to 03170. It's a Defence tab. This is from Satish Nambiar to Goulding, dated the 30th of January, 1993. So this, Mrs. Negga, is precisely the same day as the letter we were just looking at, 30th of January, 1993. And it says there at point 1: "We have kept headquarters fully informed of developments in the area since 22 January 1993 when the Croatian government resorted to unilateral use of force."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we try to blow up the English a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Since then," and this is again at paragraph 1, Mrs. Negga, "since then the military situation that is been relatively --" there's a sentence I missed. "Since then, despite various calls for a cessation of operations, and assurances received, operations have continued until late afternoon 28 January 1993 when the Peruca dam was retaken by the Croatian Army. Since then, the military situation has been relatively quiet - I would say ominously so." Now, reading that, does that remind you that at the end of January there was a major Croatian offensive in Sector South, an offensive into the protected area of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I would have learnt of that afterwards, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, it does say here that the attack started on the 22nd. Do you think by the 30th you -- well, let me ask you. Do you remember anything at all during the time, after the time? Can you remember that there was a major offensive in Sector South --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: It was on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could please go to the last page of this document. This is a press report which apparently is attached to Mr. -- General Nambiar's report from Reuters, dated the 30th of January, again the same day as Mr. Hadzic's letter. It says: "Croatian President Franjo Tudjman said in an interview published on Saturday his troops were ready to continue attacking Serb forces even if caused the collapse of the Geneva peace talks. He said he would withdraw the mandate of UN peacekeeping troops in Eastern Slavonia in March unless UN soldiers disarmed Serb units there and repatriate Croatian refugees. Then we will act on our own. Croatia will always take steps to protect its entire territory. The Serbs must accept defeat or suffer more defeats." And then down at the bottom it says: "We are only liberating our own country." Now did you understand or know at the time that Croatia's position was that, if necessary, it would retake the protected areas by force?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: With my dealings with the Croatian officials, they were under the impression that UNPROFOR was there to return the territory to them, the occupied areas to them, and their threats were mainly centred on the return of the refugees to the occupied areas. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that impression correct as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that part of the Vance Peace Plan that those territories would be returned to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And isn't it right that the whole idea of the Vance Plan is that the UN protected areas, the fate, the ultimate fate, would be determined through further negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to paragraph 48 of your statement. And here you say -- I'm not sure whether you have it in front of you, Mrs. Negga. Your statement, paragraph --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Paragraph 48 says -- you describe your first encounter with the local RSK authorities on 10 June 1992, and then you say: "Furthermore, these RSK authorities said clearly that they would not allow non-Serb returnees back into the sector." And then you refer to two documents down there in the footnote, and I would like to turn to those two documents. Could we start by looking at Prosecution tab 12, 05182. This is Prosecution tab 12. I'm not sure whether Mrs. Negga has it with her in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's not included in the selected items. I do have a copy, and I'd just remind Mrs. Negga that it's a double-sided copy. So perhaps it can be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is one of the two documents cited in your footnote. If we go to page 2, you say the atmosphere and the meeting was presided over by Milan Ilic, and it was attended by Dr. Milorad Visic, president of the Executive Board, and Milan Milanovic, deputy minister of defence of the so-called Republic of Krajina: "The atmosphere was marked by cordiality and expression of co-operation were repeatedly stressed." Do you remember that that was indeed the atmosphere of the meeting, that it was cordial and there were repeated expressions of co-operation?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes. It was my first meeting, and I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could turn over to the next page, it says: "At both meetings questions concerning the disarming of the police, military, and civilians were raised. Replies were met with snickering and general skepticism." Now, we'll get to the snickering and the skepticism, but I first of all want to focus on the three groups that you identify there as having been armed, and you mention the police and you mention the military. Can I first ask you who do you mean when you refer to the military here?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: There was the police, and then above the police you had another force, more along the line of territorial force, and that, I think, was my description of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in addition to police and military, civilians were armed?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes. They had arms all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say they were "all over the place." Do you mean to say that it was your observation that a great many civilians had weapons?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by weapons do you mean long-armed, long-barrelled weapons, such as rifles?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Well, the rifles were mostly in the possession of the military and the groups, you know, the paramilitary groups. They had APCs and other types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did civilians also have hunting rifles, for example, Thompsons, Kalashnikovs? Did you know whether those weapons were in the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I recall having read in one or two of the CIVPOL reports that there were such weapons, but I did not see them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what were the people attending snickering and skeptical about?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: We were there to implement the Vance Plan, which was to disarm the population, demilitarise the forces, and have arms under a double-lock system, and then bring the opposing forces to the table to negotiate how they will proceed. And I -- I suppose many did not agree that they should be disarmed, so there was general snickering.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And it says here: "Another question asked in Tenja concerned UNPROFOR's role in the return of refugees. There was some degree of hostility in the stance of the questioner. The message was quite that those who had left will not be allowed to return." Did you understand that whoever -- well, first of all, do you know who said that? Can you remember whether -- distinguish between the speakers at this meeting? Which one may have expressed that view?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I can't recall it off the top of my head. If it's in my notes it's what it was, but I cannot tell you from the top of my head now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you remember -- again, I know it's been a very, very long time, Mrs. Negga, and I mean no offence by asking these questions, I simply want to know what you can remember. Can you recall whether they said that these individuals, whoever had left, could never come back --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Or was it that they were saying that for as long as there was no settlement of the negotiation process, that they wouldn't be allowed to return?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I got the impression that they would never be allowed to return. There was never an additional condition added about the negotiation process. It was clear these people will not be allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by "these people," did they convey that that meant every person of Croat ethnicity or non-Serb ethnicity, or were they referring to a subset of that group; for example, people who had actually participated in hostilities? Was any such distinction drawn at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No, none was drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If they were so categorical in saying that people of non-Serb ethnicity could never return, as you say, then can you tell us why they were asking questions about UNPROFOR's role in the return of refugees - it's noted there - and why were questions asked to UNHCR about the method it proposed to return individuals?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: UNHCR certified whether an area was ripe for the return of refugees, whether there was sufficient order and calm, and whether these refugees could be resettled. In other words, UNHCR was the lead agency in the return of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the people you were speaking to at this meeting were inquiring, were they not, about UNHCR's conditions for return of non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: I -- could you rephrase -- could you repeat that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sure. I'm sorry if it wasn't clear. It's just that the last sentence of this paragraphs suggests to me, and I may be wrong and I'm seeking your assistance, that the people on the Serb side, your interlocutors, were inquiring about the conditions on which -- or the methods by which people would be returned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: No, they were not interested in the return at all. So why would they be interested in the method?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, Mrs. Negga, but -- but that is what's mentioned there in the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: What sentence is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Where it says -- and it's actually really both sentences. The first sentence begins, "Another question concerned UNPROFOR's role," and then the last sentence, "In the return of refugees," and then the last sentence says, "UNHCR was questioned as to the method it proposed to return these people."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: May I ask a question. I see Mrs. Negga trying find the page number. Perhaps that may be helpful if she knew which page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps the easiest thing is just to look at the screen, Mrs. Negga. That paragraph beginning "At both meetings."

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think it's all answered in the three sentences. "The message was quite clear that those who had left will not be allowed to return."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was it also UNPROFOR's position in 1992, given the security situation that those who had been displaced should not return for the time being?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Well, UNPROFOR had to abide by UNHCR and ICRC's advice, because they were the ones who were responsible for the conditions and the return of the refugees, so we had no say in the matter. We had to say, you know, is it right? Can -- is the time right for them to return?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So does that mean -- are you saying that UNHCR advised against returns at this time?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Mrs. Negga, this is the end of today's hearing. We will expect you back in the courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00, when we will finish your testimony. In the meantime, you're not released as a witness, and that means that you're not allowed to talk to anyone about your testimony, and you're not allowed to talk to any of the parties. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.
